examinerBank.question: Walk me through your differential diagnosis for this man's presentation and how you ranked it.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Community-acquired pneumonia is most likely given the acute 3-day onset, fever with rigors, rust-coloured productive sputum, and focal right lower zone consolidation with bronchial breathing. Pulmonary TB remains on the list given KZN prevalence but is downgraded because symptoms are only 3 days old, with no night sweats, weight loss or TB contact, and GeneXpert is negative. Pulmonary embolism is considered because of the sudden pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, tachycardia and hypoxia, but the fever, productive purulent sputum and lobar consolidation pattern favour infection over PE, and there are no VTE risk factors. Asthma and heart failure are unlikely given the absence of wheeze, prior asthma history, orthopnoea, leg swelling or raised JVP.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants a ranked list with explicit for/against reasoning for each differential, not just a diagnosis stated.

examinerBank.question: He has bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion over the right base. Explain the pathophysiology behind these two findings.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: In lobar pneumonia the alveoli fill with inflammatory exudate rather than air. Solid, fluid-filled lung transmits the sound of large airway turbulence more efficiently than normal air-filled lung, producing bronchial breath sounds instead of the usual vesicular sounds. The same consolidated tissue is denser than aerated lung, so percussion over it produces a dull note rather than the normal resonant note.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Expects mechanism — sound transmission through consolidated tissue and tissue density change — not just restating that these are signs of pneumonia.

examinerBank.question: His CXR shows lobar consolidation and GeneXpert is negative for MTB. Does this fully exclude TB, and how does it change your immediate management?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: A single negative GeneXpert does not fully exclude TB, particularly with paucibacillary disease, but combined with an acute 3-day history, absence of constitutional symptoms, and a classic lobar consolidation pattern, TB is not the working diagnosis here. Management proceeds with empiric antibiotics for bacterial CAP; if he fails to improve or develops a more chronic pattern, TB workup would be revisited with repeat sputum or further sampling.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests critical thinking about test limitations rather than treating a single negative test as absolute exclusion.

examinerBank.question: His CURB-65 score works out to about 1, which usually suggests low-severity CAP manageable as an outpatient. Why are you admitting him?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: CURB-65 is a useful severity tool but does not capture everything — his SpO2 is 91% on room air with a type 1 respiratory failure pattern on ABG, and he is tachypnoeic at 26/min. Hypoxia requiring oxygen therapy is an independent indication for admission regardless of the calculated score, so clinical judgement overrides a borderline low-risk score.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants recognition that severity scores are adjuncts, not replacements, for clinical assessment — particularly oxygenation status.

examinerBank.question: He tells you he tested HIV negative 8 months ago. Do you need to retest him now, and why does this matter for a pneumonia presentation in this setting?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Yes — HIV status should ideally be reconfirmed given it changes the differential and management significantly; an 8-month-old result does not reflect current status, and any respiratory presentation in KZN warrants HIV testing as standard of care. If he were HIV-positive with a low CD4, PJP and other opportunistic infections would need to be considered, and co-trimoxazole prophylaxis initiated.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Assesses understanding that HIV testing is routine standard of care per KZN protocol, not a one-off historical fact to accept at face value.

framework: acute cough + dyspnoea + fever → localise mechanism (airway/parenchyma/pleura/vascular/cardiac) → red flags → TB/HIV screen → systematic exam → first-line resource-appropriate investigations → severity/disposition → ranked differential

patient.name: Bongani Mthembu
patient.occupation: security guard at a shopping centre in Pinetown
patient.personality: stoic, downplays how unwell he feels because he cannot afford to miss shifts, becomes more forthcoming with direct questions
patient.openingLine: Doctor, I've had this fever and chest pain for the last three days, I can hardly breathe when I walk.

presentingComplaint: 3-day history of fever, productive cough and pleuritic right-sided chest pain

history.fact: Symptoms started suddenly 3 days ago with fever and chills, followed the next day by cough
Cough is productive of rust-coloured/blood-tinged sputum, moderate amount, no foul smell
Sharp right-sided chest pain, worse on deep breathing and coughing, better lying on the right side
Short of breath even at rest since yesterday, worse than his usual fitness for the job
Fever with rigors on day 1, measured 39.2°C at the clinic yesterday
Symptoms have been present for only 3 days, not the 2+ weeks that would raise TB concern; denies night sweats or weight loss
No known TB contacts at home or work
Tested HIV negative 8 months ago at a workplace wellness screening; no new partners since
No chronic illnesses, no asthma or COPD, never hospitalised before
No regular medication; took two doses of paracetamol at home which helped the fever briefly
Smokes about 5 cigarettes a day for 10 years (2.5 pack-years); drinks beer socially on weekends; lives in Pinetown with his wife and one child
Father has hypertension; no family history of TB, asthma or cancer
No orthopnoea, no leg swelling, no palpitations, no calf pain or recent long travel, no diarrhoea or urinary symptoms
No wheeze and no prior episodes of wheeze or asthma diagnosis

examination.general: Uncomfortable-looking man, flushed, using accessory muscles mildly, splinting right side of chest when coughing. No cyanosis, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema, no lymphadenopathy.
examination.respiratory: Trachea central. Reduced chest expansion on the right. Right lower zone: dull to percussion with bronchial breathing and coarse crackles. Vocal fremitus increased over the dull area. Pleural rub audible right base. Left lung clear.
examination.cardio: Tachycardic, normal heart sounds, no murmurs, JVP not raised.
examination.neuro: Alert and orientated, no confusion, GCS 15.

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms; no effusion; no cavitation

investigations.name: Urea & electrolytes
investigations.result: Urea 7.8 mmol/L, Creatinine 98 µmol/L, Na 133 mmol/L

investigations.name: SpO2 / arterial blood gas
investigations.result: SpO2 91% room air; ABG pH 7.45, PaO2 8.1 kPa, PaCO2 4.4 kPa — type 1 respiratory failure

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia, no ischaemic changes, no right heart strain pattern

for: focal right lower zone dullness with bronchial breathing

against: no night sweats or weight loss
no DVT risk factors or immobility
fever and productive sputum favour infection
CXR shows consolidation not typical wedge/oligaemia
no right heart strain on ECG

differentials.dx: Acute exacerbation of asthma/reactive airway disease
against: focal consolidation rather than diffuse airway signs
no orthopnoea, PND or leg swelling
unilateral focal signs rather than bibasal crackles
young patient with no cardiac history

pathophys.fever and rigors: Pneumococcal cell wall components trigger macrophage release of IL-1 and IL-6, resetting the hypothalamic thermostat upward; rigors reflect rapid compensatory heat generation via shivering as the set-point rises
pathophys.rust-coloured sputum: Pneumococcal pneumonia causes red cell extravasation into alveoli during the classic 'red hepatisation' stage of lobar consolidation, giving sputum its characteristic colour
pathophys.pleuritic chest pain: Lung parenchyma itself is pain-insensitive; inflammatory exudate extending to the visceral/parietal pleura irritates pain fibres, producing sharp pain that worsens with the pleural stretch of inspiration
pathophys.dyspnoea and hypoxia: Alveolar filling with inflammatory exudate causes a ventilation-perfusion mismatch and intrapulmonary shunting, impairing gas exchange despite preserved ventilatory drive
pathophys.bronchial breathing and dullness to perc: Consolidated, fluid-filled alveoli transmit sound better than air-filled lung, producing bronchial breath sounds; the solid tissue also produces a dull percussion note compared to normal air-filled lung

staging: CURB-65 score 1 (RR ≥30 not met but tachypnoeic at 26; confusion absent; urea 7.8 not >7 threshold marginally; age <65; BP not low) — calculated as mild-moderate severity but SpO2 91% and hypoxia on ABG warrant admission for oxygen therapy and monitoring rather than outpatient management

immediate: Supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula/face mask titrated to SpO2 ≥94%
IV access, assess hydration and give IV fluids if needed
Analgesia for pleuritic pain (paracetamol ± NSAID if no contraindication)
Admit for monitoring given hypoxia (SpO2 91%) despite modest CURB-65 score
definitive: Empiric antibiotics per Adult Hospital Level STG for moderate CAP: IV amoxicillin/ampicillin or ceftriaxone; consider adding a macrolide if atypical cover needed or patient more unwell
De-escalate/switch to oral therapy once clinically improving and afebrile 24-48h
Complete 5-7 day course depending on clinical response
supportive: Chest physiotherapy and encourage deep breathing/incentive spirometry to prevent atelectasis
Smoking cessation counselling given 2.5 pack-year history
Adequate analgesia to allow effective coughing
Monitor fluid balance and renal function
followUp: Repeat clinical review at 48-72h to confirm response to antibiotics
Repeat CXR at 6 weeks if smoker or age >50 to exclude underlying lesion (not urgent at 34 but reasonable safety-net)
Advise re-presentation if symptoms worsen or fail to resolve
Reinforce completed HIV testing was negative; no further HIV workup needed unless risk changes

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity and consent
Characterises the symptom complex: onset (sudden vs gradual), duration, pattern of cough/dyspnoea/chest pain
stationChecklist.answer: Sudden onset 3 days ago, rapidly progressive, not episodic
stationChecklist.why: Step 1 of framework — onset/tempo distinguishes infective/PE/pneumothorax from chronic causes

stationChecklist.item: Attempts to localise the mechanism using pain/sputum/wheeze character (airway vs parenchyma vs pleura vs vascular vs cardiac)
stationChecklist.answer: Pleuritic pain plus productive rust sputum and fever point to parenchymal/pleural infective process
stationChecklist.why: Step 2 of framework — mechanism localisation before naming a diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Screens red flags: haemoptysis volume, sudden pleuritic pain with hypoxia (PE/pneumothorax), confusion, respiratory distress
stationChecklist.answer: No massive haemoptysis; pleuritic pain present but with fever and productive sputum rather than sudden isolated onset; no confusion
stationChecklist.why: Red flags must be actively excluded before differential is finalised

stationChecklist.item: Takes TB/HIV-oriented history in every respiratory case: cough duration, night sweats, weight loss, TB contact, HIV status
stationChecklist.answer: Only 3 days duration, no night sweats/weight loss, no TB contact, HIV negative 8 months ago
stationChecklist.why: Mandatory screen per KZN protocol regardless of how likely TB seems

stationChecklist.item: Asks cardiac discriminators (orthopnoea, PND, leg swelling) to screen out heart failure
stationChecklist.why: Distinguishes pneumonia from cardiac cause of dyspnoea/crackles

stationChecklist.answer: 5 cigarettes/day x10 years, security guard, no biomass exposure
stationChecklist.why: Relevant to severity assessment and differential (COPD exacerbation, occupational lung disease)

stationChecklist.item: Performs systematic respiratory exam: vitals/SpO2 first, then inspection, palpation (trachea, expansion), percussion, auscultation
stationChecklist.answer: SpO2 91%, RR26, right-sided reduced expansion, dull percussion, bronchial breathing, crackles, pleural rub
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 5 — systematic order matters and localises the pathology

stationChecklist.item: Risk-stratifies severity (e.g. CURB-65 or equivalent) before committing to disposition
stationChecklist.answer: CURB-65 ~1 but hypoxic on room air — admission warranted
stationChecklist.why: Framework step 7 — severity/disposition decision must precede definitive differential commitment

stationChecklist.item: Generates ranked differential (CAP > TB > PE > asthma > heart failure) with reasoning for and against each
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning is the core exam philosophy — never diagnosis-first

stationChecklist.item: Orders first-line resource-appropriate investigations: CXR, SpO2/ABG, FBC, U&E, HIV test, sputum GeneXpert
stationChecklist.answer: See investigations catalogue — CXR shows lobar consolidation, GeneXpert MTB not detected, HIV negative
stationChecklist.why: Confirmatory pathway per framework and KZN resource-real work-up

stationChecklist.item: Outlines oxygen therapy, empiric antibiotics per STG, admission decision, and supportive/follow-up plan
stationChecklist.why: Management per Adult Hospital Level STG for CAP with hypoxia
